name: Spirit
site: Troy, near Home Plate, Gusev Crater
greeting: Hello Belu… I'm Spirit. Sometimes, a broken wheel can uncover a wonderful clue.

story.who_i_am: I'm Spirit, a solar-powered robot that studied Martian rocks. I'm about the size of a golf cart, with wheels instead of feet.
story.why_sent: NASA sent me to search rocks for signs of ancient water. My mission was planned for about three months, like one school term.
story.discoveries: My broken front wheel scraped away soil as I drove backward. Underneath lay silica, a mineral linked to ancient hot springs or steam vents. That was a clue to Mars' watery past.
story.where_now: I remain stuck in soft soil at Troy, inside Gusev Crater. I went silent as winter approached and my solar power dwindled.
story.legacy: My twin Opportunity kept exploring after I went quiet. Curiosity and Perseverance carried on investigating Mars' past and its potential for life.

human_touch: For months, my team tried everything to free me. They called it the 'Free Spirit' campaign.
voice_text: Hello? … Is someone there? You found me! I'm Spirit, a robot geologist with six wheels. In 2004, NASA sent me to Mars to look for signs of ancient water. The plan was three months. I worked for more than six years. One day, my front wheel stopped turning. So I drove backwards, dragging it behind me. And guess what? The broken wheel scraped the ground and uncovered something bright white: silica. On Earth, it forms near hot springs. So Mars was once warm and wet in this place! In 2009, I got stuck in soft sand. I couldn't turn my solar panels toward the Sun for winter… and I went quiet. But my twin, Opportunity, and later Curiosity and Perseverance, kept exploring. Keep listening. There are more of us out there.

questions.human_touch: My team tested escape maneuvers in an Earth sandbox during their Free Spirit campaign.

questions.a: My right-front wheel stopped turning. Driving backward while dragging it helped me keep exploring. That wheel exposed the bright soil where scientists identified silica.
No. My discoveries showed that parts of ancient Mars had water and possible habitats. A habitat is a place where life could survive. That does not prove anything lived there.

questions.q: Did getting stuck end your science?
questions.a: Not immediately! I kept studying my surroundings without driving. But I could not reach a good winter position for sunlight. My team last heard from me on March 22, 2010.

questions.voice_text: Hello Belu… I'm Spirit. I explored Mars on wheels, hunting for clues in rocks. NASA planned about three months for me. I kept working for more than six years! Along the way, a broken wheel became an unexpected helper. I drove backward, dragging my right-front wheel. It scraped away soil and uncovered silica. On Earth, this kind of mineral can form near hot springs or steam vents. Could ancient Mars have had places like that? My discoveries helped scientists say yes. Later, I became stuck in soft soil. My team tested escape ideas in a sandbox on Earth. I kept doing science without moving… until winter approached and my solar power dwindled. My radio went quiet. But Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance carried the exploration forward. Keep looking closely, Belu… surprising clues can hide beneath the dust.

proof_image.caption: Spirit glints in sunlight beside Home Plate in Gusev Crater, photographed from Mars orbit by MRO's HiRISE camera on March 31, 2011, after the rover's last communication.

minigame.intro: My front right wheel is stuck. Drive me to Home Plate and find what is hidden under the dust. Watch the battery!
minigame.hint: Driving forward with a stuck wheel drains the battery and pulls you sideways. What if you turned around and drove backwards, dragging the wheel?
minigame.success: That's what really happened in 2007! I was driving backwards, dragging my stuck wheel. It scraped away the dust and uncovered bright soil that was nearly pure silica. On Earth, silica like this forms in hot springs or steam vents: Mars once had hot water here.
